newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgia adopts '97 budget, but IMF lending unclear.
newsitem.headline: Georgia adopts '97 budget, but IMF lending unclear.

text.p: Georgia's parliament approved a $687 million budget for 1997 on Friday which envisaged a considerably lower deficit than in 1996.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) had demanded that the budget be adopted by Friday to allow Georgia to receive the next tranche of an $80 million credit vital for the stability of the Caucasus republic's currency, the lari.
But it remained unclear whether approval of the budget would be enough to secure continued IMF lending.
Hunter Monroe, IMF representative in Georgia, said it was premature to comment on loan disbursals.

He said an IMF delegation would arrive in the republic over the next two weeks to study the budget and make recommendations on the disbursement of future credits, most of which are used to plug Georgia's deficit.

"If the evaluation is favourable, then the delegation will advise the IMF board of directors meeting on March 19 to make a postive decision," he told Reuters. "I think it would be premature to say anything else at this time," he said.

Parliament voted overwhelmingly to approve the budget, which calls for 1997 spending of 886.1 million lari. Revenues are projected at 686.1 million lari, leaving a deficit of 200 million lari. The 1996 deficit was around 300 million lari.
"This is a real breakthrough in the building of a market economy," Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze told parliament after the budget was approved.
The budget envisages 378 million lari going to social needs, by far the largest spending category. Defence spending is put at 90 million lari, education at 51 million and culture 30 million.
Social spending was nearly double last year's levels.
Two-thirds of revenues are to be made up from taxes collected from the private sector.
